topic: IBM 1410 core architecture (storage, character format, addressing, indexing, registers, instruction formats, chaining, word marks, arithmetic/compare model, Priority feature, 1401 compatibility) for a TypeScript functional emulator
summary:
The IBM 1410 (1411 Processing Unit) is a variable-word-length, character-addressed, decimal machine. Storage is offered in five models: 10,000 / 20,000 / 40,000 / 60,000 / 80,000 character positions (Models 1–5, "A" suffix = fifth E frame). Each position holds a BCD character with bits B A 8 4 2 1, plus a word-mark (WM) bit and a check (odd-parity C) bit; parity is computed over BA8421+WM. 64 code points exist; the collating sequence is blank=00 lowest through 9=63 highest (Figure 2 of the PrincOps gives the full table and card codes). Special characters relevant to control: record mark (‡, BCD A82), group mark (⧧, BA8421), word separator (~, 0-5-8 card code), and the group-mark-with-word-mark (GM-WM) that terminates I/O records. Addresses are always FIVE decimal digits, 00000 to as high as 79999 on an 80K system, so no zone encoding is needed to reach high addresses (unlike the 1401's 3-character addresses). Zone bits over the hundreds and tens positions of an address instead select one of 15 index registers (A-bit over tens = 1, B over tens = 2, A over hundreds = 4, B over hundreds = 8; sum = index register number, none = no indexing). Index registers live in core at 00025–00029 (IR1) through 00095–00099 (IR15), 5 chars each; the factor's sign is taken from its units-position zone bits and is added algebraically to the address after it enters the address register; word marks in the index area are ignored; overflow during indexing does not set the arithmetic overflow latch; the result must be a valid address or an address check stop occurs. Zone bits in the units, thousands or ten-thousands address positions are invalid; only characters with a 0–9 numeric total are legal in an address (a "&", "$", "#" cause an address check). Address 00000 is valid only for incrementing operations; the top address (e.g. 59999 on 60K) only for decrementing ones, with a console and read/write-to-end-of-core exception.

Registers: IAR (instruction address register, 5 chars, steps by one per character read; reset/program reset load 00001), AAR and BAR (5-char A- and B-address registers; they are decremented per character when a field is addressed by its low-order end, incremented when addressed by the high-order end), CAR (C-address register, used by Store Address Register, multiply, divide, table lookup; not programmer-visible except via G), DAR (multiply/divide/recomplement scratch), EAR and FAR (channel 1 and 2 I/O address registers, overlap feature), STAR (storage address register, indirect access to core via any address register). Single-character registers: A-data register, B-data register (8-bit: BCD + C + WM), Op register (7 bits, WM dropped), Op-modifier register (holds d-character), I/O channel select, Unit Select and Unit Number registers per channel, and channel E1/E2, F1/F2 data registers. Addresses in registers are held in two-out-of-five code and retranslated to BCD on store. Instruction forms (exact lengths, PrincOps p.11): O (1), O d (2), O xxx d (5), O aaaaa (6), O aaaaa d (7), O xxx bbbbb d (10), O aaaaa bbbbb (11), O aaaaa bbbbb d (12). The first character (op) must carry a word mark; the instruction contains no other word marks; the WM on the next instruction's op code terminates instruction read-out. Instruction-length validity is checked (Instruction Check light). Chaining: a one-character instruction reuses AAR and BAR left from the previous operation; a 6-character form of a two-address instruction supplies only A and chains the B-address, and "uses the last previous operation modifier"; an 11-character instruction blanks the op-modifier register, so subsequent chained ones get a blank d. Each instruction description tabulates IAR/AAR/BAR after the operation (e.g. Add two-field: NSI, A-LW, B-LB; Compare: NSI, A-LW, B-LW; unconditional branch: IAR=NSIB, AAR=BI, BAR=NSIB; one-address conditional branch not taken: IAR=NSI, AAR=BI, BAR=BI; two-address branch not taken: AAR=BI, IAR=NSI, BAR=B-1). On a taken branch the old IAR (the NSIB) is placed in BAR, the branch address moves from AAR into STAR, and IAR = branch address + 1 after the op is read; storing BAR with G (C) B in the subroutine captures the return address.

Arithmetic (add-to-storage, no accumulators): fields are addressed at their units (rightmost) position and processed right to left; the B-field's word mark defines the field length and stops the operation. The A-field needs a word mark only if it is shorter than the B-field, in which case zeros are added/subtracted into the remaining high-order B positions; if A is longer, its excess high-order positions are simply not processed (no error). Sign is in the units-position zone bits: B-bit only = minus (11 zone); no zones, B+A (12 zone), or A only (0 zone) = plus. The machine generates B+A for plus and B for minus. Zone bits in other positions of B are preserved; A-field zones are ignored except in the units position. True-add vs complement-add per Figure 12; the sign of the result of a complement add is the sign of the greater value (after the A sign is changed for subtract). Characters whose numeric bits exceed 9 or have no numeric bits are treated as: blank/&/-/substitute blank -> 0, others drop the 8 bit (e.g. # (821) -> 3; group mark -> G or 7). Overflow: carry out of the high-order B position is lost and the arithmetic overflow indicator turns on (add/subtract only; it is not set by ZA/ZS/multiply/divide); tested and reset by J (I) Z or a computer reset. Zero balance: set when the result of add, subtract, ZA, ZS or multiply is zero; reset by the next such operation (except divide) with a non-zero result; tested by J (I) V (branch does not reset it). Divide overflow is a separate indicator (J (I) W; division by zero always sets it). Compare (C): compares B to A character by character from the units end using BA8421 bits only (not C or WM), ended by the first word mark in either field; sets B>A (high), B=A (equal), B<A (low) and unequal indicators according to the collating sequence; if the A-field is shorter, high is turned on; if the B-field is shorter or equal length the results are correct for the compared portion; negative fields compare as ordinary characters (e.g. 4444444D > 4444444M in the example set). The four compare indicators are reset by the next compare, table lookup, or branch-if-character-equal; computer reset turns on low and unequal. Table lookup (T) also sets compare indicators. The Priority feature (Special Feature 5620, Extension 5621) is an interrupt system: when in priority alert mode (entered by Y (I) E, exited by Y (I) X or by an interrupt) and a priority request indicator turns on (overlap, I/O unit, inquiry, outquiry, seek, attention — per channel), the system, while reading the op code of an interruptible unchained instruction, branches to 00101 and leaves priority alert mode; the priority routine stores BAR, subtracts 6, and uses that as the I-address of the Y (I) E that returns to the main program. Test-and-branch Y (I) d instructions with d = 1,2 (overlap ch1/2), U,F (I/O unit), Q,* (inquiry), N,‡ (outquiry), S,T (seek), A,B (attention). 1401 compatibility: a console COMPATIBILITY toggle (1410/1401) puts the machine in 1401 mode; a 10K 1410 acts as an 8K 1401, larger ones as a 16K 1401; supported 1401 features include Advanced Programming (indexing, SAR, move record), multiply-divide, expanded print edit, print storage, high-low-equal compare, sense switches (console sense-bit switches A–G); differences listed on PrincOps pp.98–100 (invalid parity input becomes * instead of being corrected; quotient blanks converted to zeros; card read buffer lags; BAR differs after card/print ops, e.g. read leaves 082 rather than 081; single-character edit differs). No storage-protection feature appears anywhere in the 1410 PrincOps (A22-0526-3 or May-63 edition TOC); it is a 7010 feature (unverified here). The 1410 Accelerator feature shortens the core cycle from 4.5 to 4.0 µs but changes no semantics.

facts.claim: Five 1411 models: Model 1/1A = 10,000; 2/2A = 20,000; 3/3A = 40,000; 4/4A = 60,000; 5/5A = 80,000 storage positions. Suffix A models have a fifth (E) frame. Core cycle is 4.5 µs per character (4.0 µs with the 1410 Accelerator).
facts.source: IBM 1410 Principles of Operation, Form A22-0526-3, p.5 and p.96 — https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

facts.claim: Character format: BCD bits B A 8 4 2 1, plus a word-mark bit and a check bit. Parity is odd over BA8421 plus WM; the check bit is added when the count of BA8421+WM bits is even. Examples on p.5: A (BA1) no WM -> C not added -> 'BA1'; A with WM -> 'WMCBA1' (check bit added); C (BA21) no WM -> CBA21; X (A421) with WM -> WMA421.

There are 64 code points; collating sequence is ascending from blank (00) to 9 (63); Figure 2 (p.6) lists every character with card code and BCD bits. Key controls: record mark ‡ = A 8 2 (card 0-2-8); group mark = B A 8 4 2 1 (card 12-7-8); word separator ~ = C A 8 4 1 (0-5-8); substitute blank = C A (2-8); & = C B A (12); - = B (11).
facts.source: A22-0526-3 p.6 Figure 2 'Standard BCD Interchange Code' — https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

facts.claim: Word mark functions: (1) marks the first character (op code) of an instruction, (2) defines the size of a data field, (3) signals the end of an instruction. Every instruction must be followed by a word mark (the next op's WM) which stops instruction reading. Word marks remain until changed by clear storage, clear word mark, set word mark, or a data move that specifies WM transfer.

Addresses are 5 characters, valid 00000 up to 79999 on an 80K system. No zone-bit encoding is needed for the address magnitude (unlike the 1401). Zone bits are permitted only in the tens and hundreds positions (index tags); any zone bits in the units, thousands or ten-thousands positions make the address invalid; any position without a 0–9 numeric total (e.g. &, $, #) is invalid. Legal characters in tens/hundreds: numerals, letters, and / ? ! ‡.

Boundary rules: for decrementing operations 00001 is the lowest usable position; addressing 00000 in a decrementing op stops with an address-check error (no exceptions). 00000 is always valid for incrementing ops. For incrementing ops, the top address minus 1 (59998 on 60K) is the highest usable; the top address (59999) causes an address check except for console display/alter and read/write 'to end of core' I/O. The top address is valid for decrementing ops.

Address registers: IAR, AAR, BAR (programmer visible), CAR (used by Store Address Register G, multiply, divide, table lookup; not programmer accessible), DAR (multiply/divide/recomplement), EAR/FAR (channel 1/2 overlap I/O), STAR (storage address register; all storage access goes through it). Address characters are translated to two-out-of-five code before entering an address register; more or fewer than two bits per character = address channel error. Contents are retranslated to BCD when stored by G.

IAR: 5-character instruction counter. Holds the op-code address at start of read-out; increased by one each storage cycle during instruction read; at end of read-out holds the op address of the NSI. Changed by (1) console load, (2) normal stepping, (3) successful branch: branched-to address plus one replaces IAR during execution of the branched-to instruction, (4) program reset / computer reset loads 00001.

AAR/BAR: 5-character registers holding the addresses of the units positions (normally) of data fields. After each character is acted on the address is decreased by one (field addressed at low-order) or increased by one (addressed at high-order, i.e. left-to-right record moves and I/O). BAR holds the I/O address during non-overlapped I/O.

Single-character registers: B-data register (8-bit: BCD, check, WM; loaded on every storage read-out and written back on regeneration), A-data register (8-bit, loaded from B-data register when needed), Op register (7 bits, WM bit dropped), Op-modifier register (7-bit d-character), I/O channel select (hundreds position of x-control), Unit Select (tens) and Unit Number (units) per channel, E1/E2 and F1/F2 channel data registers.

Instruction form: Op (1 char), A-address or I-address (5) or x-control field (3), B-address (5), d-character (1). Valid lengths: O=1, O d=2, O xxx d=5, O aaaaa=6, O aaaaa d=7, O xxx bbbbb d=10, O aaaaa bbbbb=11, O aaaaa bbbbb d=12. Instruction-length checking is performed per op code (Instruction Check light).
facts.source: A22-0526-3 p.11 'Instruction Form' and 'Instruction Length Validity' — https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

facts.claim: Instruction word marks: each instruction must have a WM over the op code and must not contain WMs elsewhere; a WM must be set in the location immediately right of the last character (normally the next instruction's op). That WM stops instruction read-out.

x-control field (I/O instructions M, L, U, F, etc.): hundreds position selects channel and overlap mode (% = ch1 non-overlap, @ = ch1 overlap, ⌑ (lozenge) = ch2 non-overlap, * = ch2 overlap); tens = device type (1 reader, 2 printer, 4 punch, U tape, T console printer, B tape odd-parity, F disk, etc.); units = unit number / specific operation. x-control fields and G instructions cannot be indexed.
facts.source: A22-0526-3 p.11, p.14, p.92, p.105 Figure 107 — https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

facts.claim: Chaining: an op code alone reuses the AAR/BAR contents left by the prior instruction (e.g. after A 05985 06985 with LA=5, LB=6, AAR=05980, BAR=06979; a following bare S subtracts 05980 field from 06979 field). If a two-address instruction does not require a d-character (11-char), the op-modifier register is blanked, so chained instructions after it get a blank d. For D, W, B, V, T (two-address ops with d) 'an instruction length of 6 chains the B-address and uses the last previous operation modifier'.
facts.source: A22-0526-3 p.12 'Chaining Instructions', p.25, p.30, p.38 — https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

facts.claim: Branch register effects. If branch occurs: after read-out IAR has stepped; IAR (the NSIB) is transferred to BAR; AAR holds the branch address, which goes to STAR during read of the branched-to instruction and IAR = that address + 1 thereafter. So a G (C) B in the subroutine stores the return address. If no branch (two-address branch): AAR=BI, IAR=NSI, BAR=B-1 (allows re-testing the next lower position by chaining). If no branch (one-address branch): AAR=BAR=BI, IAR=NSI. Unconditional branch J (I) blank: IAR=NSIB, AAR=BI, BAR=NSIB.

Fifteen index registers occupying core 00025–00029 (IR1), 00030–00034 (IR2), ... 00095–00099 (IR15), i.e. IRn at 00020+5n through 00024+5n. Selected by zone bits on the tens and hundreds address positions: value = (A over tens ? 1 : 0) + (B over tens ? 2 : 0) + (A over hundreds ? 4 : 0) + (B over hundreds ? 8 : 0); 0 = no indexing. A-, B- and I-addresses can each be tagged independently.

Indexing semantics: the index factor is a 5-digit number added algebraically (sign from units-position zone bits of the factor; B-bit = minus; no bits or BA = plus) to the address after it enters the address register and before execution; the instruction in storage is not changed. Word marks in 00025–00099 are ignored by indexing; zone bits in the index registers are undisturbed and ignored except in the units (sign) position. Arithmetic overflow latch is NOT set by indexing overflow. Result must be a valid address or the system stops with an error. On a 10K system the high-order position of an address being indexed must contain zero. Cost: 34.5 µs per address indexed (30.67 with Accelerator). Examples p.15 (e.g. A-address 009Z6 = 00996 tagged IR1 with factor 0001J = -00011 -> 00985).

Sign representation: sign determined by zone bits in the units position. Minus = B bit only (card 11 zone). Plus = no zone, B and A (12 zone), or (less commonly) A only (0 zone). When the machine generates/changes a sign it writes B+A for plus and B for minus.
facts.source: A22-0526-3 p.16 'Sign Change or Development', Figure 11 — https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

facts.claim: Add/subtract cycle type (Figure 12): Add with like signs = true add, result sign = common sign; unlike signs = complement add, result sign = sign of greater value. Subtract first inverts the A-field sign then adds. Digit coding: characters with numeric bits totalling 0–9 (numerals, letters, / ? ! ‡) are used by value; blank, &, -, substitute-blank become 0; other specials (8+2, 8+4 etc.) drop the 8 bit (e.g. # (821) -> 3, group mark BA8421 -> 7, or 'G' if zones retained).

Field-length governance for A/S/ZA/ZS (two fields): the B-field word mark stops the operation and defines the length. The A-field needs a word mark only if it is shorter than B; then zeros are added/subtracted (or zeroed for ZA/ZS) into B's remaining high-order positions up to and including the WM position. If A is longer than B, the excess high-order A positions are not processed. B-field zone bits are unchanged except in the sign position; A-field zone bits are ignored except in the sign position. Registers after: IAR=NSI, AAR=A-LW, BAR=B-LB (LW = length of shorter field).

Overflow: if the result exceeds the B-field limit (B word mark) the carry is lost and the arithmetic overflow indicator turns on; tested and turned off by J (I) Z (BAV); also reset by computer reset. Overflow can be detected only in add and subtract, not ZA, ZS, multiply, divide.

Zero balance: turned on if the result of any add, subtract, multiply, ZA or ZS is zero; turned off by the next arithmetic instruction (any except divide) whose result is non-zero; tested by J (I) V (BZ). Also reset by computer reset.

One-field forms: A (A) image-adds the field to itself (doubling), S (A) subtracts from itself (zeroes numerics, zones unchanged), ZA (A) strips zones except sign and forces B+A for plus, ZS (A) strips zones except sign and reverses the sign. Registers after: NSI, A-LA, A-LA.
Zero and Subtract two-field sign table (Figure 13): A no B/no A (plus) -> B minus (B bit); A B-bit (minus) -> B plus (B and A); A B+A (plus) -> B minus; A A-only (plus) -> B minus.

Multiply @ (A)(B): A = multiplicand (units-addressed), B = product field whose high-order positions initially hold the multiplier image; B-field length must be LA + LM + 1; product replaces multiplier; sign = product of signs placed in units of B; zones in multiplicand undisturbed. Divide % (A)(B): A = divisor (units-addressed), B-address = LEFTMOST position of the dividend; B-field length = L(divisor) + L(dividend) + 1; quotient develops in leftmost positions, remainder in rightmost; dividend must be signed in its units position; divide overflow indicator (J (I) W) on divide by zero or improperly addressed dividend; registers after: NSI, A-LA, tens position of quotient field.

Compare C (A)(B): compares B to A character by character on BA8421 bits only (not C or WM), collating per Figure 2; sets high (B>A), equal (B=A), low (B<A), and unequal (on with either high or low). Ended by the first word mark in either field. If A is shorter than B, the high indicator is turned on (example 5, even when the compared portions are equal). If B is shorter or equal, indicators correctly reflect the compared portion. Negative values compare as characters (example 6: 4444444D vs 4444444M -> B high). Indicators reset by next compare, table lookup, or branch-if-character-equal; computer reset turns off zero result and turns on low and unequal. Registers after: NSI, A-LW, B-LW.

Conditional one-address branch J (I) d, with d: Z overflow, 9/! carriage 9 ch1/ch2, R/L carriage busy, @/⌑ carriage overflow 12, S equal, U high, T low, / unequal, W divide overflow, Q/* inquiry request ch1/ch2, 1/2 overlap in process, K tape indicator (CE), V zero balance. Registers: branch IAR=NSIB, AAR=BI, BAR=NSIB; no branch IAR=NSI, AAR=BI, BAR=BI. Length 1 or 7.

Branch if I/O channel status indicator on: R (I) d for channel 1, X (I) d for channel 2; d bits: 1 not ready, 2 busy, 4 data check, 8 condition, B-bit (‘-’) wrong length record, A-bit (substitute blank) no transfer; group mark (all bits) tests all six. Branch if any bit in d matches. An R/X status test (branch, or R (I) group-mark) must follow each I/O instruction on a channel before the next, else the channel interlock stops the system. Indicators reset at the beginning of the next I/O operation.
facts.source: A22-0526-3 p.37–38 Figure 36; Priority bulletin p.8 — https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf

facts.claim: Two-address branches: B (I)(B) d = branch if character at B equals d (BA8421 compare, WM and C excluded; also sets high/low/equal indicators); W (I)(B) d = branch if any bit of B-char matches any bit of d; V (I)(B) d = branch if word mark present (d bit 1) and/or zone test (d bit 2 with B/A zones: 1 WM, 2 zones absent, B zones=BA, K zones=B, S zones=A, 3 WM or no zones, C WM or BA, L WM or B, T WM or A). Length 1, 6 or 12; 6 chains the B-address and prior d. Registers: branch NSIB/BI/NSIB; no branch NSI/BI/B-1.

Move D (A)(B) d: d bits 1 = transfer numeric portion, 2 = zone portion, 4 = word marks, none = scan only; 8-bit set = left-to-right (record) move, terminating on A-field record mark (A-bit), A-field GM-WM (B-bit), either (A and B bits), or first WM in either field (no A/B); 8-bit off = right-to-left field move terminating after one position (no A/B), A-field WM (A-bit), B-field WM (B-bit), first WM in either (A and B). Full 64-entry table Figure 22 p.27. Registers per Figure 20 (e.g. R-to-L stop at either WM: A-LW, B-LW; L-to-R record mark: A+LA, B+LA).

Move Characters and Suppress Zeros Z (A)(B): A-field WM defines length; high-order zeros and commas in B replaced by blanks; sign zone bits removed from B units; B-field WMs within the area including leftmost are removed. Registers after: NSI, A-LA, B+1.

Table lookup T (A)(B) d: A = search argument (units-addressed, WM at leftmost), B = rightmost char of table; each table field has function (leftmost) + argument (rightmost) with a WM at the field's leftmost; d = 1 low, 2 equal, 3 low/equal, 4 high, 5 low/high, 6 equal/high, 7 any, blank = to end. Stops one position left of matching argument; BAR = address of rightmost function char; AAR = A-LW; sets compare indicators; a short table field ends the search with high indicator on.

Processing-control ops: G (C) d — Store Address Register (d = A, B, E, F) stores the register at the C-address (rightmost) without changing AAR; cannot be indexed; 69.75 µs; registers after NSI, Ap, Bp. Set Word Mark ',' (A)(B) and Clear Word Mark ⌑ (A)(B): one or two addresses or chained; registers A-1, B-1. Clear Storage / (B): clears data and WMs from B down to nearest hundreds boundary, BAR=bbb00-1 (e.g. / 12590 clears 12590–12500, BAR=12499); with I-address = clear storage and branch. Halt '.' (length 1) or Halt and Branch . (I). NOP N: any length.

Computer reset: resets check circuits, IAR to 00001, timing clocks, and all machine indicators (overflow latches, compare triggers etc.); program reset: check circuits, IAR to 00001, A/B data registers, Op and Op-modifier registers, console inquiry latch.

Priority Feature (Special Feature 5620; Extension 5621 adds channel 2 I/O unit/inquiry/outquiry): interrupt system providing an automatic branch to storage location 00101 when a priority request indicator turns on while the system is in priority alert mode. Entering alert mode: Y (I) E (BEPA), which also branches; exit: Y (I) X (BXPA) or the interrupt itself. Interrupt happens during instruction read-out, before execution, and only for unchained, interruptible op codes at interruptible lengths (Figure 1: ? ! A S @ % E Z C / ' ⌑ at length 11; W V D B T at 12; J R X at 7; Y N M L G . U F K never). The request indicator turning on also turns off alert mode.
facts.source: IBM 1410 Priority Feature, Form A22-0530-1, pp.3–5 — https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0530-1_1410_priorityFea.pdf

facts.claim: Priority request indicators per channel: overlap (Y(I)1 / Y(I)2; set at completion of an overlapped read/write/write-check, reset by R(I)d / X(I)d), I/O unit (Y(I)U / Y(I)F; set by priority select switch device finishing, or priority select on-off key), inquiry (Y(I)Q / Y(I)*), outquiry (Y(I)N / Y(I)‡), seek (Y(I)S / Y(I)T), attention (Y(I)A / Y(I)B). Return from the priority routine: store BAR (which holds the interrupted instruction address + read-out steps), subtract 6, and use it as the I-address of the Y (I) E at the end of the routine. Arithmetic/compare indicators are not saved automatically.

I/O NOP instruction (Priority feature only): M/L x x x BBBBB d with d = Q (input status) or V (output status); identical to a read/write but no data transfer; used to set the I/O channel status indicators for the device that interrupted.

1401 compatibility: a COMPATIBILITY toggle on the 1415 console CE panel (1410 / 1401) puts the machine in 1401 mode (1401 COMPAT light). A 10K 1410 runs as an 8K 1401; all larger 1410s run as a 16K 1401. Supported 1401 features: additional storage, multiply-divide, expanded print edit, advanced programming (indexing, SAR, move record), print storage, high-low-equal compare, read-punch release, sense switches. NOT supported: column binary, compressed tape, punch feed read, serial I/O adapter units, process overlap, selective tape listing, space suppression.

1401-mode behavioural differences: bad-parity input becomes '*' rather than being corrected; blank quotient positions are converted to zeros; 1410 does not put the 1401 set-up character in 000/100 after read/punch; BAR after card/print ops differs (read: 1401 081 vs 1410 082; print 333 vs 335; punch 181 vs 183); 1402 EOF not reset by new deck (only computer reset); 8-2 card punch reads as A-bit (1401 reads it invalid); in load mode the 1410 writes two word separators per WM on tape and reads a pair as one separator without setting a WM; single-character edit is transferred by the 1410 but not the 1401; 1311 BAR ends at least one greater; 51-column read fills positions 1–14 and 66–80 with blanks.

Processing overlap / Data Channel 2 are special features; each channel has E1/E2 (ch1) or F1/F2 (ch2) data registers and EAR/FAR address registers; the x-control hundreds character selects channel and overlap; only M and L ops with x1 (or x4 console) can overlap; at end of an overlapped read EAR is two positions right of the last stored character (checking for GM-WM). Both channels can overlap simultaneously; a non-overlap op on one channel converts the other's overlap to non-overlap; channel 1 has priority on simultaneous requests.

The 1410 Principles of Operation (A22-0526-3, 1961 reprint incorporating TNL N22-0169-0; and the A22-0526 October-1962 major revision with pages revised 5/1/63) contain no storage-protection section in the table of contents or the System Features chapter; the 1410 as documented has no storage protection feature.
facts.source: A22-0526-3 p.3 contents, pp.92–100; A22-0526 May-63 p.3 contents — https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526-3_1410_princOps.pdf , https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-0526_1410_princOpsMay63.pdf

facts.claim: Storage protection existed as a feature on the IBM 7010 (the 1410's faster successor), not on the 1410.
facts.source: memory; 7010 PrincOps A22-6726 at https://bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/1410/A22-6726_7010_PrincOps.pdf not read in this session

facts.claim: Edition/form numbers: A22-0526-3 (reprint of A22-0526-2 + TNL N22-0169-0, ©1960/1961, 111 pages); A22-0526 'Major Revision October 1962' with pages revised 1/15/63 (TNL N22-0070) and 5/1/63 (TNL N22-0083), obsoleting the earlier Reference Manual A24-1407-1/-2 and TNLs N22-0030 (1401/1410 compatibility), N22-0032 (overlap), N22-0045 (accelerator), N22-0054, N22-0059. Priority Feature bulletin is A22-0530-1 (©1962, obsoletes A22-0530-0). Page numbering in both PrincOps PDFs matches printed page numbers (PDF page N = printed page N).
Console 1415 sense-bit switches A–G act as program-testable sense switches only in 1401 mode; the 1410 mode has no sense switches.

open_questions: Exact state of IAR/BAR at the moment of a priority interrupt (bulletin says 'store BAR and decrement by six' to get the return address for Y(I)E; the precise register snapshot for each interruptible op length should be confirmed against the CE manual 1410_CE_Manual_Oct61.pdf or the 1410 System Fundamentals 223-2589).

1401-mode address decoding: in 1401 mode the 1410 must interpret 3-character 1401 addresses (with zone bits encoding thousands, the 1401 scheme); the PrincOps compatibility section (pp.98–100) does not spell out the mapping or how 16K-1401 addresses map onto 1410 core — needs the TNL N22-0030 '1401/1410 Compatibility' or the CE manual.
Move Characters and Edit (E) rules (p.31–35) were not read in this pass.

Whether the May-1963 edition (A22-0526, pages revised 5/1/63) changes any of the addressing/indexing/chaining rules relative to A22-0526-3 (its contents page shows re-paginated sections, e.g. Indexing p.19, Compatibility p.95); diff not performed.
Storage protection on the 7010 (A22-6726) — asserted from memory only; verify before relying on it for a 7010 mode.
Exact behaviour of the Address Check when an indexed address overflows into an invalid value on 20K/40K/60K systems vs wrapping (manual says 'system will stop on an error').
